Collèges privés et inégalités de revenus en France

Niveau global ou ségrégation spatiale ?

Author

Camille Favre

Published

October 1, 2026

Micrometrics

1 Introduction

In 2025, 21% of French collège (lower-secondary) students are enrolled in a private school under contract with the State. This share varies substantially across académies (figure Figure 1); for example, in the Rennes académie, 43% of lower-secondary students are in a private institution, but this share drops to 11% in the Limoges académie.

NoteShare of students passing Brevet (last year of lower-secondary) from a private institution by académie

We may think that this difference is linked with the social and economic composition of the city. But is it mostly linked with the global level of inequalities, or with spatial segregation? Indeed, spatial segregation may already select students based on parental socio-economic status — a form of selection that private collèges offer, decreasing the need for private lower-secondary schools. On the other hand, depending on the intensity of spatial segregation, some streets may be composed only of rich households and others only of poor households, both assigned to the same public school, increasing the demand for private schools. Which dimension of income inequality matters for the presence of private lower-secondary schools within a city in France: its overall level, or its spatial segregation?

We use French administrative data on collèges (Annuaire de l’éducation, IPS, Valeur ajoutée) matched with income data at the 200m grid-cell level (Filosofi). With Filosofi, we construct indicators such as Theil and Moran indices to capture the level of inequality of each city. We then estimate count models on the number of private schools in each city, including controls and académie fixed effects.

Being in a school composed of good students may positively affect your own results: if the behavior of your peers impacts your academic performance, you may have incentives to seek out schools with the best students. This behavior affects both the offer and the demand for private schools. @epple1998 build a theoretical model showing that in the presence of peer effects, private schools discriminate through the tuition price in order to select the best and the richest students (cream-skimming). This prediction is well supported empirically (@epple2004).

However, this theoretical paper does not explain the impact of the spatial distribution within a city on the offer of private schools. In the French system, public lower-secondary schools are subject to strict catchment-area assignment; hence, the supply of private schools may significantly change depending on the level of spatial segregation of the catchment area.

2 Methodology

2.1 Measuring inequality within cities: Theil and Moran indices

2.1.1 Filosofi cells

Filsosofi provides 200m grid-cell level that gives us information on the mean income, the number of persons, the poverty rate, the share of people in a given age group, the share of land-owners, … A city is composed of different cells, each one having at maximum 8 neighbor cells. We can see a city as a network of these cells.

Here we provide an example with Rennes.

First we can visualize the network of Rennes (Figure 2). We can see some ‘cliques’ (independant group of only few cells), this is normal when we look at the administrative map of Rennes (Figure 3) since we do have some few cells ‘alone’ (but that had neihbooring cells without Rennes). In some case we don’t have any cell, that’s because of the statisticall secret, if there are not enough people in the cell, INSEE does not provide any information.

NoteNetwork of Rennes with 200m cells
NoteAdministrative map of Rennes with 200m cels

2.1.2 Measuring inequality within cities: Theil and Moran indices

To disentangle the level of inequality from its spatial structure, we build two complementary indicators from the Filosofi income data at the 200m grid-cell level. We illustrate their construction with the real grid of Rennes.

2.1.2.1 Theil index: overall inequality

The Theil index belongs to the family of generalized entropy indices and measures the overall dispersion of income within a city. For a city \(c\) composed of \(N_c\) grid cells, with mean income \(\bar{y}_c\) and income of cell \(i\) denoted \(y_i\):

\[ T_c = \sum_{i=1}^{N_c} \omega_i \, r_i \ln r_i, \qquad r_i = \frac{y_i}{\sum_{j} \omega_j y_j}, \]

where \(\omega_i\) is the population share of cell \(i\) (so that \(\sum_i \omega_i = 1\)) and \(r_i\) its income relative to the city mean. The index is zero when all cells have identical income and increases with dispersion. Its two appealing properties for our purpose are (i) scale invariance — it does not mechanically grow with the average income level of the city — and (ii) exact decomposability:

\[ T_c = \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} \omega_g T_g}_{\text{within-group}} + \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} \omega_g \ln\left(\frac{\bar{y}_g}{\bar{y}_c}\right)}_{\text{between-group}}, \]

where \(g\) indexes groups of cells (e.g. neighborhoods), \(\omega_g\) is the population share of group \(g\), and \(\bar{y}_g\) its mean income.

2.1.2.2 Moran’s I: spatial segregation

The Moran statistic measures spatial autocorrelation: whether cells with high (resp. low) income are neighbors of cells with high (resp. low) income. Define the row-standardized spatial weights matrix \(W = (w_{ij})\), where \(w_{ij} = 1\) if cells \(i\) and \(j\) are within 285 m of each other (the 8 adjacent 200 m cells) and \(w_{ij} = 0\) otherwise, row-standardized so that \(\sum_j w_{ij} = 1\). With \(z_i = y_i - \bar{y}_c\) the deviations from the city mean:

\[ I_c = \frac{N_c}{S_0} \cdot \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N_c} \sum_{j=1}^{N_c} w_{ij} \, z_i z_j}{\sum_{i=1}^{N_c} z_i^2}, \qquad S_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{N_c} \sum_{j=1}^{N_c} w_{ij}. \]

The index lies in \([-1, 1]\): \(I_c \to 1\) when cells of similar income cluster together (segregated city), \(I_c \approx 0\) when incomes are spatially random, and \(I_c \to -1\) under a checkerboard pattern.

2.1.2.3 The two indices applied to Rennes

Voir le code 
# Mêmes données et mêmes paramètres que le Code 2 : carreaux Filosofi
# 200 m, voisinage intra-communal 285 m, recours kNN pour les isolés.
library(sf); library(spdep); library(dplyr)

os_name <- Sys.info()[["sysname"]]
if (os_name == "Windows") {
  dossier_donnees <- "G:/Mon Drive/Education/Master APE 25-27/Mémoire/Données MicroMetrics/france_metro/"
} else if (os_name == "Darwin") {
  dossier_donnees <- "/Users/camillefavre/Mon Drive/Education/Master APE 25-27/Mémoire/Données MicroMetrics/france_metro/"
} else stop("Système d'exploitation non pris en charge.")

gpkg_path <- paste0(dossier_donnees, "carreaux_200m_met.gpkg")
CODE <- "35238"   # Rennes

rennes <- st_read(gpkg_path,
  query = sprintf("SELECT * FROM carreaux_200m_met WHERE lcog_geo LIKE '%s%%'", CODE),
  quiet = TRUE) %>%
  filter(is.finite(ind) & ind > 0 & is.finite(ind_snv)) %>%
  mutate(revenu = ind_snv / ind)                       # €/uc par carreau
Voir le code 
DIST_VOISIN <- 285; K_KNN <- 4; NSIM <- 499
set.seed(2025)

# --- Fonctions identiques au Code 2 ---
weighted_theil <- function(x, w) {
  ok <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(w) & x > 0 & w > 0
  x <- x[ok]; w <- w[ok]; w <- w / sum(w)
  rel <- x / sum(w * x)
  sum(w * rel * log(rel))
}

# --- Voisinage intra-communal (285 m, kNN pour les isolés) ---
xy <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_transform(rennes, 2154)))
nb <- dnearneigh(xy, d1 = 0, d2 = DIST_VOISIN)
if (any(card(nb) == 0)) {
  knnb <- as.list(knn2nb(knearneigh(xy, k = min(K_KNN, nrow(xy) - 1))))
  nbl  <- as.list(nb)
  for (j in which(card(nb) == 0)) nbl[[j]] <- knnb[[j]]
  nb <- structure(nbl, class = "nb", region.id = attr(nb, "region.id"), sym = attr(nb, "sym"))
}
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

y  <- rennes$revenu
wt <- rennes$ind

# --- Theil (pondéré par la population, comme au niveau France) ---
T_rennes   <- weighted_theil(y, wt)
ybar_rennes <- weighted.mean(y, wt)

# Contribution de chaque carreau au Theil
rel_i  <- y / sum((wt / sum(wt)) * y)
contrib_i <- (wt / sum(wt)) * rel_i * log(rel_i)

# --- Moran global (test par permutation) ---
mi <- moran.test(y, lw, zero.policy = TRUE, randomisation = TRUE)
I_rennes <- mi$estimate[1]
p_rennes <- mi$p.value

# --- Quadrants LISA (typologie exhaustive, sans filtre, comme Code 2) ---
z  <- as.numeric(scale(y))
wz <- lag.listw(lw, z, zero.policy = TRUE)
rennes$quadrant <- ifelse(wz >= 0, ifelse(z >= 0, "HH", "LH"),
                                ifelse(z >= 0, "HL", "LL"))

# --- Décomposition des contributions au Theil ---
part_top5  <- sum(sort(contrib_i, decreasing = TRUE)[1:floor(0.05 * length(contrib_i))]) / T_rennes
part_LL    <- sum(contrib_i[rennes$quadrant == "LL"]) / T_rennes

# --- Orthogonalité : mêmes revenus, positions permutées ---
y_perm    <- sample(y)
T_perm    <- weighted_theil(y_perm, wt)
I_perm    <- moran.test(y_perm, lw, zero.policy = TRUE)$estimate[1]

res_rennes <- list(N = nrow(rennes),
                   ybar = ybar_rennes, T = T_rennes, I = as.numeric(I_rennes),
                   p = p_rennes, part_top5 = part_top5, part_LL = part_LL,
                   T_perm = T_perm, I_perm = as.numeric(I_perm),
                   y_max = max(y), y_min = min(y))

The mean disposable income per consumption unit in Rennes is 24751 € across 824 grid cells (incomes range from 12037 to 40695 €). The Theil index of the city is \(T_{\text{Rennes}} = 0.0262\), and the Moran statistic is \(I_{\text{Rennes}} = 0.431\) (permutation test, \(p = 0.000\)).

Two facts summarize the division of labor between the indices:

  1. Theil aggregates, Moran locates. The 5% most unequal-contributing cells account for 120 of the Theil index, but the Theil is blind to where they are. The Moran statistic is the one that tells us that rich cells (Thabor, the city center) and poor cells (Le Blosne, Villejean) each stand next to similar cells, rather than being spatially interlaced — figure Figure 4 shows this in a single scatter: the slope of the fitted line is the Moran statistic.

  2. The indices are orthogonal by construction. Permuting the incomes across the cells of Rennes leaves the distribution — hence the Theil index — strictly unchanged (\(T = 0.0210\), identical to \(0.0262\)), while the Moran statistic collapses to \(I = -0.028\): without spatial structure, there is no autocorrelation left. In the count model of private collèges, the coefficient on \(T_c\) therefore captures the demand driven by the overall dispersion of income, while the coefficient on \(I_c\) captures the additional effect of the spatial clustering of rich and poor households within the same catchment areas.

NoteMoran scatterplot of Rennes: each cell’s income against its neighbors’
NoteLISA typology of Rennes: where the clusters are

2.2 Count data estimation

To answer this economic question we use count data model. Indeed, the dependent variable is the number of private lower secondary school within a city. This positive integer describe an intensity, justifying a count data model.

Voir le code 
freq %>%
  mutate(Sum = cumsum(Share)) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 1,
    col.names = c("Private lower secondary schools", "Communes", "Share (%)", "Cumulative (%)")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)

The mean of this distribution is 1.38 and the variance is 4.82 (figure Figure 6). We can seee that we clearly have overdispersion, hence, using a Poisson model would be innapropriate here.

NoteDistribution of private lower secondary schools per city
Voir le code 
moy <- mean(d$nb_colleges_prives, na.rm = TRUE)
var_y <- var(d$nb_colleges_prives, na.rm = TRUE)
ratio <- var_y / moy
n0  <- sum(d$nb_colleges_prives == 0, na.rm = TRUE)

distrib <- d %>%
  filter(!is.na(nb_colleges_prives)) %>%
  count(n = nb_colleges_prives, name = "nb_communes") %>%
  mutate(n = pmin(n, 5)) %>%
  group_by(n) %>%
  summarise(nb_communes = sum(nb_communes), .groups = "drop")

y_max <- max(distrib$nb_communes)

p <- ggplot(distrib, aes(x = n, y = nb_communes)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8", width = 0.68) +
  # --- moyenne (ligne pointillée) ---
  geom_vline(xintercept = moy, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#B4562A", linewidth = 0.55) +
  annotate("text", x = moy + 0.12, y = y_max * 0.97,
           label = sprintf("Mean = %.2f", moy),
           color = "#B4562A", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold") +
  # --- boîte variance / surdispersion (haut droit) ---
  annotate("text", x = 4.95, y = y_max * 0.97, hjust = 1,
           label = sprintf("Variance = %.2f\nVar / Mean = %.2f\n(overdispersion)",
                           var_y, ratio),
           color = "#1a1a2e", hjust = 1, size = 3.5, lineheight = 1.1,
           fontface = "bold") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:5,
                     labels = c("0","1","2","3","4","5+"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05)),
                     labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "Number of private lower secondary schools per city",
       y = "Number of cities",
       subtitle = sprintf("N = %s cities · %.1f%% of cities have none",
                          scales::comma(nrow(d)), 100 * n0 / nrow(d))) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    axis.text          = element_text(color = "black", size = 11),
    axis.title         = element_text(color = "black", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle      = element_text(color = "grey30", size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "grey88", linewidth = 0.3),
    axis.line          = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.4)
  )

p

Indeed in a poisson distribution we have : \[ y_i \mid x_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i), \qquad \mu_i = \mathbb{E}(y_i \mid x_i) = \mathbb{V}(y_i \mid x_i) \tag{1}\]

In our data, however, \(\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(y_i \mid x_i) < \widehat{\mathbb{V}}(y_i \mid x_i)\): the variance is 4.82 for a mean of 1.38, revealing substantial overdispersion.

To adress the issue of surdispersion, we should add a disturbance term to the parameter : \(\log \left(\mathbb{E}(y_i \mid x_i)\right) = x_i \theta + \epsilon\), so that the probability is \[ \mathbb{P}(y_i = k \mid x_i, u_i) = \frac{e^{-\mu_i u_i} (\mu_i u_i)^{y_i}}{y_i !}, \quad \quad \quad u_i = \log(\epsilon) \] In order to get a closed form solution (Greenwood & Yule 1920) proposed to use a Gamma distribution with mean 1 for \(u_i\) \[ u_i \sim \frac{\alpha^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}e^{-\alpha u_i}u_i^{\alpha-1} \] In that case, \[ \mathbb{P}(y_i = k \mid x_i) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha + k)}{\Gamma(k + 1)\Gamma(\alpha)}r_i^{k}(1-r_i)^{\alpha-1}, \qquad r_i = \frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_i + \alpha} \]
